hints: Remember what Kp means, it is products over reactants using partial pressures, not concentrations.
Look at the balanced equation and spot which gas has a big 2 in front of it, that number becomes a power.
Check that the product pressure is on top and each reactant pressure is raised to its balancing number on the bottom.
walkthrough:
**Recall the rule for Kp**

Think products on top, reactants on bottom. Each partial pressure is raised to the power of its balancing number in the equation.

$$K_p = \frac{\text{(product pressures)}}{\text{(reactant pressures)}}$$

**Apply it to this equation**

The product is $\text{CH}_3\text{OH}$ with no number in front, so it is just $p_{\text{CH}_3\text{OH}}$ on top. The reactants are $2\text{H}_2$ and $\text{CO}$, so the bottom is $(p_{\text{H}_2})^2 \times p_{\text{CO}}$.

$$K_p = \frac{p_{\text{CH}_3\text{OH}}}{(p_{\text{H}_2})^2 \times p_{\text{CO}}}$$

**Avoid the coefficient trap**

The 2 in front of $\text{H}_2$ becomes a power of 2, it never goes inside the bracket as $2p$. That gives the correct expression straight away.

options.A: This is upside down and misuses the 2. Kp must have products on top, but here reactants are on top. Also $(2p_{\text{H}_2})^2$ is wrong, the 2 is a power, not a multiplier inside.
options.B: This is upside down. It puts reactants $(p_{\text{H}_2})^2 \times p_{\text{CO}}$ on top and product $p_{\text{CH}_3\text{OH}}$ on the bottom. Kp is always products divided by reactants.
options.C: Correct. Product $p_{\text{CH}_3\text{OH}}$ is on top, and reactants are on the bottom with $p_{\text{H}_2}$ squared because of the 2 in $2\text{H}_2(g) + \text{CO}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{OH}(g)$.
options.D: The top and bottom are the right way round, but $(2p_{\text{H}_2})^2$ is wrong. The balancing number becomes an exponent only, so it should be $(p_{\text{H}_2})^2$, not $2p$ squared.
